nameStory: Purpletop vervain gets its name from the distinctive purple-tinged flower clusters that crown its tall stems. The word 'vervain' comes from the Latin 'verbena,' which was used for sacred plants in ancient Roman ceremonies - these plants were considered so holy they were used to sweep Jupiter's altar!
description: Purpletop vervain is a tall, slender wildflower that can reach 3-6 feet in height with an upright, branching growth habit. This South American native produces small purple flowers arranged in dense, elongated clusters at the tips of its stems. The plant has a somewhat weedy appearance with narrow leaves and a tendency to form colonies in disturbed areas. It's quite rare in New England, with only one confirmed observation recorded in the region.

idTips.label: Flowers
idTips.description: Tiny purple flowers packed densely into narrow, spike-like clusters at stem tips that feel firm and slightly rough to the touch, blooming from bottom to top of each spike

idTips.label: Leaves
idTips.description: Narrow, lance-shaped leaves arranged opposite each other on the stem, with serrated edges that feel slightly rough and sandpapery when rubbed

idTips.label: Growth Habit
idTips.description: Tall, upright plant with multiple branching stems that create an open, airy appearance, often swaying gently in the breeze

idTips.label: Seeds
idTips.description: Small, dry seeds develop in tiny capsules along the flower spikes, creating a textured, bumpy feel when the flowers fade

habitat: Based on its extreme rarity in New England, purpletop vervain likely appears in disturbed soils, roadsides, or areas with human activity where seeds might be accidentally introduced. Like other vervains, it probably prefers sunny locations with well-drained soil. Given its South American origin, it may struggle with New England's harsh winters and is likely found only as an occasional escapee or temporary introduction.

seasonality.spring: New growth emerges as the weather warms, with distinctive opposite leaves appearing on upright stems.
seasonality.summer: Peak blooming period with characteristic purple flower spikes fully developed and most obvious for identification.
seasonality.fall: Flowers fade and seeds develop, with dried flower spikes persisting and plant beginning to decline with cooler temperatures.
seasonality.winter: Plant likely dies back completely in New England's harsh winters, surviving only if seeds germinate the following spring.

funFact: This vervain was only officially described as a distinct species in 1995, making it one of the most recently named plants you might encounter - younger than many smartphones and discovered after the invention of the Internet!
confusionNotes: Most likely confused with blue vervain, but purpletop vervain has much denser, more compact flower spikes and tends to be taller and more slender overall. Memory trick: 'Purple-top' has tighter tops than blue vervain's loose, branching flower clusters.
contextualKnowledge: Don't confuse this purpletop vervain (Verbena incompta) with the more common purpletop vervain (Verbena bonariensis) - they're different species with the same common name! The extremely low observation count suggests this plant is either very rare, misidentified, or represents occasional introductions that don't establish permanent populations.
compareHints: Unlike the common blue vervain with its loose, branching flower clusters, purpletop vervain has much denser, more compact purple spikes. It's also typically taller and more slender than white vervain, and lacks the fuzzy, grayish appearance of hoary vervain. The tight, cylindrical flower spikes are the key feature separating it from most other vervains in the region.

relatedSpecies.distinction: Among its vervain relatives, blue vervain is the tallest and wetland-loving member of the family in New England.
White vervain stands out among New England's vervains for its pure white flowers and extremely thin flower spikes.
Unlike our native blue vervain which prefers wet meadows and has blue flower spikes, purpletop vervain is much taller with distinctly flat-topped purple flower clusters.
Unlike its upright cousins blue vervain and white vervain which grow several feet tall, bigbract verbena hugs the ground in spreading mats.
Among the vervains in New England, hoary vervain is the only one with distinctly fuzzy, grayish foliage - all the others have smooth or only slightly hairy bright green leaves.
Common vervain stands out from its New England relatives by having the thinnest, most delicate flower spikes in the vervain family.
Among New England vervains, narrowleaf vervain is distinguished by having the thinnest leaves and most delicate appearance.
Unlike its taller New England verbena cousins like blue vervain (which grows 3-5 feet tall with spiky flower clusters), moss verbena stays low to the ground with dense, rounded flower heads.
